# Sign in with bWalletX

How to let people sign in to your site or app with their bWalletX: one script tag, two routes on your server, and no API keys.

Also as plain Markdown for AI coding agents: [bwalletx.com/connect.md](https://bwalletx.com/connect.md). Checked against bWalletX 5.1.82, connect.js and @bsv/sdk 2.8.11 on 7 Oct 2026.

## In 30 seconds

One script tag on your page, two routes on your server.

``<script src="https://bwalletx.com/connect.js"></script>
``

- `bWalletX.renderButton('#signin', { onClick })` draws the gold "Sign in with bWalletX" button.

- `bWalletX.signIn({ challenge, pairing })` finds the user's wallet (Chrome extension, the bWalletX app's browser, or a phone or the web wallet by QR code), asks your server for a one-time challenge, and has the wallet sign it with a key derived from its identity key.

- Your server checks the signature with `@bsv/sdk`, deletes the nonce, and signs the user in as that identity key.

- No API key, no client ID, no account with us. Nothing passes through bwalletx.com except the script itself. The only service of ours involved is the encrypted pairing relay, and only when the user signs in from a phone or the web wallet.

The user's identity key (a 33-byte compressed public key, 66 hex characters) is their user ID on your site. It is the same key every time they sign in with the same wallet.

## Three ways the user's wallet can answer

Where the user is
How your page reaches the wallet
What you need

Chrome or Brave with the bWalletX extension
BRC-100 wallet discovery: dispatch `brc100:requestWallet`, take the `brc100:announceWallet` reply whose `info.rdns` is `com.bwalletx.extension`
Nothing extra. connect.js finds it

Your site opened inside the bWalletX app's own browser
Same discovery; the app announces `rdns: space.bwallet.mobile` and also sets `window.CWI`
Nothing extra. connect.js finds it

bWalletX on a phone, or the web wallet at web.bwalletx.com
Pairing: your page shows a `https://www.bwallet.space/pair?...` link as a QR code. The phone scans it; the web wallet takes it pasted. Both then talk to your page through `relay.bwallet.space`, end-to-end encrypted
A `pairing` option with somewhere to show the QR code. connect.js does the rest

All three give you the same thing: an object with the BRC-100 `WalletInterface` methods. Sign-in is the same code for all of them.

## 1. Browser: one script tag

`connect.js` is small. It loads the full sign-in build (`https://bwalletx.com/connect/bwalletx-connect.global.js`, about 125 KB with `@bsv/sdk` inside) the first time you call `signIn`, `pair` or `renderButton`, so those three return promises. This example uses qrcodejs from cdnjs to draw the QR code; any QR library works.

``<div id="signin"></div>
<div id="bwx-pair"></div>

<script src="https://bwalletx.com/connect.js"></script>
<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/qrcodejs/1.0.0/qrcode.min.js"></script>
<script>
const panel = document.getElementById('bwx-pair');

async function post(url, body) {
const res = await fetch(url, { method: 'POST', headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json' }, body: JSON.stringify(body) });
if (!res.ok) throw new Error((await res.json().catch(() => ({}))).error || 'HTTP ' + res.status);
return res.json();
}

bWalletX.renderButton('#signin', {
onClick: async (button) => {
button.disabled = true;
try {
const r = await bWalletX.signIn({
// 1. Your server makes the challenge for this identity key.
challenge: (identityKey) => post('/auth/bwalletx/challenge', { identityKey }),
// 2. Only used when there is no extension or in-app browser: phone or web wallet.
pairing: {
onLink: (link) => {
panel.replaceChildren();
new QRCode(panel, { text: link, width: 220, height: 220 });
const p = document.createElement('p');
p.textContent = 'Scan with bWalletX on your phone, or paste this link into web.bwalletx.com: ' + link;
panel.append(p);
},
onCode: (code) => panel.append('Check bWalletX shows ' + code + ', then tap Connect.'),
},
});
// 3. Your server checks the signature and starts a session.
const { identityKey } = await post('/auth/bwalletx/verify', {
identityKey: r.identityKey, nonce: r.nonce, signature: r.signature,
});
panel.textContent = 'Signed in as ' + identityKey.slice(0, 12) + '… (via ' + r.method + ')';
} catch (e) {
panel.textContent = e.code === 'NOT_FOUND' ? 'bWalletX was not found.' : e.message;
} finally {
button.disabled = false;
}
},
});
</script>
``

`bWalletX.signIn` looks for a wallet in this order:

- The bWalletX Chrome extension (BRC-100 discovery, `rdns` `com.bwalletx.extension`). `method: 'extension'`.

- The bWalletX app's in-app browser (`rdns` `space.bwallet.mobile`, or `window.CWI` if nothing announced). `method: 'in-app'`.

- A pairing saved by an earlier sign-in in this browser (in `localStorage` under `bwalletx.connect.pairing.v1`). `method: 'pairing'`.

- A new pairing, if you passed `pairing`: `onLink` gets a `https://www.bwallet.space/pair?...` link to show as a QR code (and as text for web.bwalletx.com), and `onCode` gets a 4-digit code both screens show. `method: 'pairing'`.

If none of these works it throws an error with `code: 'NOT_FOUND'`. It returns `{ identityKey, signature, nonce, method, wallet }`. Post the first three to your verify route. `wallet` is a BRC-100 `WalletInterface` you can keep using.

Other things on `window.bWalletX`:

Call
What it does

`bWalletX.connect({ timeout })`
The extension only, authenticated: `{ wallet, info, identityKey }`. Rejects with `code: 'NOT_INSTALLED'`. Doesn't load the full build.

`bWalletX.pair({ onLink, onCode })`
A wallet paired by QR or pasted link, without signing in.

`bWalletX.renderButton(el, { onClick, subtitle })`
The gold button. `subtitle: false` hides the second line.

`bWalletX.load()`
The full build's exports (`signInWithBwalletX`, `pairBwalletX`, `restorePairing`, `clearPairing`, `findBwalletX`, ...).

Prefer to host it yourself? Copy `connect.js` and `connect/bwalletx-connect.global.js` to the same folder structure on your site; connect.js loads the full build from next to itself. It is also on npm: `pnpm add @bwalletx/connect @bsv/sdk`.

## The button

Sign in with bWalletXalso works with bWallet

`bWalletX.renderButton()` draws this for you. If you draw your own, use the gold button. Keep the label "Sign in with bWalletX". The logo is at `https://bwalletx.com/logo.svg` (the gold b, viewBox 74 x 100). Don't recolour it; it sits on a black circle so it reads on the gold.

``<button type="button" id="bwx-signin" class="bwx-signin">
<span class="bwx-mark"><img src="https://bwalletx.com/logo.svg" alt="" width="15" height="20"></span>
<span class="bwx-label">Sign in with bWalletX<small>also works with bWallet</small></span>
</button>
<div id="bwx-pair"></div>
``
``.bwx-signin {
display: inline-flex; align-items: center; gap: 12px;
min-height: 48px; padding: 10px 22px 10px 10px;
border: 0; border-radius: 12px; cursor: pointer;
background: linear-gradient(180deg, #fcd34d, #f59e0b);
color: #000; text-align: left;
font: 700 16px/1.2 system-ui, -apple-system, "Segoe UI", sans-serif;
box-shadow: 0 8px 24px rgba(245, 158, 11, 0.2);
}
.bwx-signin:hover { background: linear-gradient(180deg, #fde68a, #fbbf24); }
.bwx-signin:focus-visible { outline: 2px solid #ffd24d; outline-offset: 3px; }
.bwx-signin:disabled { opacity: 0.6; cursor: wait; }
.bwx-signin .bwx-mark {
display: inline-flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center;
width: 32px; height: 32px; border-radius: 50%; background: #000; flex: none;
}
.bwx-signin small { display: block; font-size: 11px; font-weight: 500; color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.6); }
``

Put it first among your wallet options. The second line ("also works with bWallet") is optional: bWallet is the store edition of the same wallet and signs in the same way.

## 2. Server: issue and verify challenges

The server half is not in the script (it must run on your server). Install `@bwalletx/connect` and import from `@bwalletx/connect/server`, or copy this file into your project as `bwalletx-server.ts`. Its only dependency is `@bsv/sdk` (2.2 or later, 2.x or 3.x). It is the same code as `@bwalletx/connect/server`, so the two are interchangeable.

``import { ProtoWallet, PublicKey, type WalletProtocol } from '@bsv/sdk';

/** Security level 2, a protocol name used for nothing else. Keep it constant. */
export const LOGIN_PROTOCOL: WalletProtocol = [2, 'bwallet sign in'];
export const CHALLENGE_LIFETIME_MS = 2 * 60 * 1000;

export interface PendingChallenge {
identityKey: string;
origin: string;
message: string;
expiresAt: number;
}

/**
* Where challenges wait between the two routes. Use Redis or a database table in production.
* `take` must read and delete in one step, so each nonce can be tried once.
*/
export interface NonceStore {
put(nonce: string, c: PendingChallenge): Promise<void> | void;
take(nonce: string): Promise<PendingChallenge | null> | PendingChallenge | null;
}

let warned = false;

/**
* In-memory store. For development and tests only: it is lost on restart and not shared between
* server processes or serverless instances. Expired entries are pruned on each put.
*/
export function memoryStore(opts: { quiet?: boolean } = {}): NonceStore {
if (!opts.quiet && !warned) {
warned = true;
console.warn('[@bwalletx/connect] Using the in-memory nonce store. It is for development only; pass a shared store (Redis, database) in production.');
}
const m = new Map<string, PendingChallenge>();
return {
put(nonce, c) {
const now = Date.now();
for (const [k, v] of m) if (v.expiresAt < now) m.delete(k);
m.set(nonce, c);
},
take(nonce) {
const c = m.get(nonce) ?? null;
m.delete(nonce);
return c;
},
};
}

let defaultStore: NonceStore | null = null;
const storeOrDefault = (s?: NonceStore) => s ?? (defaultStore ??= memoryStore());

export function isIdentityKey(x: unknown): x is string {
if (typeof x !== 'string' || !/^0[23][0-9a-fA-F]{64}$/.test(x)) return false;
try {
PublicKey.fromString(x);
return true;
} catch {
return false;
}
}

function normalOrigin(origin: string): string {
const u = new URL(origin);
if (u.origin === 'null' || u.origin !== origin.replace(/\/$/, '')) {
throw new Error(`origin must be scheme://host[:port], got ${origin}`);
}
return u.origin;
}

/** The text the user signs. Lines joined with \n, no trailing newline. */
export function loginMessage(origin: string, nonce: string, expiresAt: number): string {
return [
`Sign in to ${new URL(origin).host} with bWallet`,
'',
'This proves you hold this wallet. It does not spend anything.',
'',
`Origin: ${origin}`,
`Nonce: ${nonce}`,
`Expires: ${new Date(expiresAt).toISOString()}`,
].join('\n');
}

function randomNonce(): string {
const b = new Uint8Array(16);
globalThis.crypto.getRandomValues(b);
let s = '';
for (const x of b) s += String.fromCharCode(x);
return btoa(s).replace(/\+/g, '-').replace(/\//g, '_').replace(/=+$/, '');
}

export interface CreateChallengeOptions {
/** YOUR site's origin from config, e.g. "https://example.com". Never take it from the request. */
origin: string;
/** The identity key the browser claims. Checked again at verify. */
identityKey: unknown;
/** Default: a process-wide in-memory store (dev only). */
store?: NonceStore;
}

export interface ChallengeResponse {
nonce: string;
message: string;
protocolID: WalletProtocol;
keyID: string;
expiresAt: number;
}

/** Step 1. Throws if identityKey is not a valid compressed public key. Send the result to the browser. */
export async function createChallenge(opts: CreateChallengeOptions): Promise<ChallengeResponse> {
if (!isIdentityKey(opts.identityKey)) throw new Error('identityKey must be a compressed public key (66 hex chars)');
const origin = normalOrigin(opts.origin);
const nonce = randomNonce();
const expiresAt = Date.now() + CHALLENGE_LIFETIME_MS;
const message = loginMessage(origin, nonce, expiresAt);
await storeOrDefault(opts.store).put(nonce, { identityKey: opts.identityKey.toLowerCase(), origin, message, expiresAt });
return { nonce, message, protocolID: LOGIN_PROTOCOL, keyID: nonce, expiresAt };
}

export interface VerifySignInOptions {
/** YOUR site's origin from config. Must equal the origin the challenge was made for. */
origin: string;
/** From the request body. */
identityKey: unknown;
nonce: unknown;
signature: unknown;
store?: NonceStore;
}

/**
* Step 2. Returns the proven identity key (lowercase hex), or null.
* The nonce is deleted before anything is checked, so each challenge can be tried once.
*/
export async function verifySignIn(opts: VerifySignInOptions): Promise<string | null> {
if (typeof opts.nonce !== 'string' || opts.nonce.length > 64) return null;
const c = await storeOrDefault(opts.store).take(opts.nonce);
if (!c || Date.now() > c.expiresAt) return null;
let origin: string;
try {
origin = normalOrigin(opts.origin);
} catch {
return null;
}
if (c.origin !== origin) return null;
if (!isIdentityKey(opts.identityKey)) return null;
const identityKey = opts.identityKey.toLowerCase();
if (c.identityKey !== identityKey) return null;

const sig = opts.signature;
if (!Array.isArray(sig) || sig.length < 8 || sig.length > 80 || !sig.every((b) => Number.isInteger(b) && b >= 0 && b <= 255)) {
return null;
}
try {
const { valid } = await new ProtoWallet('anyone').verifySignature({
protocolID: LOGIN_PROTOCOL,
keyID: opts.nonce,
counterparty: identityKey,
data: Array.from(new TextEncoder().encode(c.message)),
signature: sig as number[],
});
return valid ? identityKey : null;
} catch {
return null; // @bsv/sdk throws on a bad signature instead of returning valid: false
}
}

/** True when a request's Origin header is exactly your configured origin. Check it on both routes. */
export function originAllowed(requestOrigin: string | null | undefined, origin: string): boolean {
try {
return !!requestOrigin && requestOrigin === normalOrigin(origin);
} catch {
return false;
}
}
``

Two routes. This example uses Express; any framework works the same way.

``// Two routes (Express). Any framework works the same way.
import express from 'express';
import { createChallenge, verifySignIn, originAllowed, memoryStore } from './bwalletx-server.js';

const ORIGIN = 'https://example.com'; // your site, from config. Never from the request.
const store = memoryStore(); // dev only: use Redis or a database table in production
const app = express();
app.use(express.json());

// POST /auth/bwalletx/challenge body: { identityKey }
app.post('/auth/bwalletx/challenge', async (req, res) => {
if (!originAllowed(req.get('origin'), ORIGIN)) return res.status(403).end();
try {
res.json(await createChallenge({ origin: ORIGIN, identityKey: req.body?.identityKey, store }));
} catch (e) {
res.status(400).json({ error: (e as Error).message });
}
});

// POST /auth/bwalletx/verify body: { identityKey, nonce, signature }
app.post('/auth/bwalletx/verify', async (req, res) => {
if (!originAllowed(req.get('origin'), ORIGIN)) return res.status(403).end();
const identityKey = await verifySignIn({ origin: ORIGIN, store, ...req.body });
if (!identityKey) return res.status(401).json({ error: 'That signature was not accepted. Start again.' });
// identityKey is the user's stable id. Find or create the account keyed on it, then start your session.
res.json({ identityKey });
});

app.listen(3000);
``

`verifySignIn` returns the identity key (66 lowercase hex characters) or `null`. It refuses a nonce that was already used, has expired (2 minutes), was issued for another origin or another identity key, or whose signature doesn't verify.

`memoryStore()` is for development: it is lost on restart and isn't shared between processes or serverless instances. In production pass a store whose `take(nonce)` reads and deletes in one step, such as Redis `GETDEL` or a database `DELETE ... RETURNING`.

## Exactly what is signed

The server builds this text, sends it to the browser, and keeps a copy. The wallet signs the UTF-8 bytes of it unchanged. Lines are joined with `\n`, no trailing newline.

``Sign in to example.com with bWallet

This proves you hold this wallet. It does not spend anything.

Origin: https://example.com
Nonce: 3q2-7wEXAMPLEnonce0Q8w
Expires: 2026-10-07T12:02:00.000Z
``

(The second and fourth lines are empty.) This is the same text bChat and bit-sign use. The wallet does not parse it; any text works, but keep your origin, the nonce and the expiry in it so the user can see what they are approving and a signature made for your site is worthless anywhere else.

The signature call, as the wallet receives it:

Field
Value

`protocolID`
`[2, 'bwallet sign in']` (security level 2: the derived key depends on the counterparty)

`keyID`
the nonce

`counterparty`
`'anyone'`

`data`
the UTF-8 bytes of the text, as `number[]`

result `signature`
DER-encoded ECDSA signature, as `number[]`

The signing key is derived (BRC-42) from the wallet's root identity private key towards "anyone", for that protocol and keyID. Anyone holding only the identity public key can derive the matching public key, which is what `new ProtoWallet('anyone').verifySignature({ ..., counterparty: identityKey })` does (BRC-3). Only the holder of the identity private key can make the signature.

## Security notes

- One try per nonce. Delete the challenge before you check the signature, as `verifySignIn` does. A challenge that survives a failed attempt can be retried.

- Two-minute expiry. Check it on the server. Don't trust an expiry sent by the browser.

- The nonce is also the keyID, so each challenge is signed by a different derived key. A signature for one nonce can't be used for another.

- Build the text on the server and verify against your stored copy. Never verify text the browser sends you.

- Use your configured origin in the text, not a value from the request. Refuse challenge and verify calls whose `Origin` header isn't your site.

- Bind the challenge to the identity key the browser claimed, and check it again at verify.

- `verifySignature` throws on a bad signature in @bsv/sdk instead of returning `valid: false`. Catch it and treat it as a failure.

- Check the key is a real point: `PublicKey.fromString` throws for a 66-hex string that isn't on the curve.

- Rate-limit the challenge route per IP and per identity key. It is unauthenticated.

- Sessions are yours. After `verifySignIn` returns a key, issue your normal session cookie. The wallet does not give you a token.

- Privacy. The identity key is the same on every site the user signs in to with this method, so two sites can tell it is the same wallet. Tell your users this if it matters to them.

- Pairing. The relay checks the WebSocket `Origin` of the page that opened the channel and tells the wallet; the wallet refuses to pair if it differs from the origin in the QR code. The relay only sees ciphertext. The pairing key connect.js makes is random and is not a wallet key.

- What the user sees. The extension and the phone show their own approval prompt naming your site's host (taken from the page or the relay, not from your text). Nothing is spent.

## Not yet available

These are gaps today. Plan around them.

- No hosted sign-in or OAuth-style redirect. There is no bwalletx.com page you can send users to and get a callback from, and no hosted verify endpoint. You run the two routes yourself. bChat's own endpoints (`/api/bitsign/auth/bwallet/*` on bit-sign) accept requests from their own pages only and are not a public API.

- No user profile. You get the identity key and nothing else: no $handle, paymail, name or picture, and no proof linking the key to them.

- The relay is ours. `relay.bwallet.space` accepts any https origin, but it is a single service run by The Bitcoin Corporation with no published uptime or rate-limit guarantees (it currently allows about 60 frames a minute per channel).

- No test wallet. There is no testnet build or headless bWalletX for automated tests. To test your server, sign with `new ProtoWallet(PrivateKey.fromRandom()).createSignature(...)` using the same arguments; it makes exactly the signature bWalletX makes.

## For AI agents

Follow these steps in order. Do not invent packages, endpoints or methods that are not on this page. For a bundled app, install `@bwalletx/connect` and `@bsv/sdk`; for a plain HTML site, use the script tag.

- Install `@bwalletx/connect` and `@bsv/sdk` in the server project (pnpm, npm or yarn, whichever the project uses).

- Create `bwalletx-server.ts` with the code in section 2, unchanged. Put your site's origin (scheme + host, no trailing slash, e.g. `https://example.com`) in config.

- Add two POST routes. `/auth/bwalletx/challenge`: `createChallenge({ origin: ORIGIN, identityKey: body.identityKey, store })`, return the result as JSON, 400 if it throws. `/auth/bwalletx/verify`: `verifySignIn({ origin: ORIGIN, store, identityKey, nonce, signature })` from the body. Reject both with 403 unless `originAllowed(request Origin header, ORIGIN)`.

- Replace `memoryStore()` with a shared store (database table or Redis) if you run more than one server process or run serverless. `take(nonce)` must read and delete in one step.

- In the verify route, when `verifySignIn` returns a key: find the user whose bWalletX identity key equals it, or create one, then start your normal session. Return 401 when it returns null.

- On the sign-in page add `<script src="https://bwalletx.com/connect.js"></script>` and the code from section 1: `bWalletX.renderButton(...)` with an `onClick` that calls `bWalletX.signIn({ challenge, pairing })` and posts `identityKey`, `nonce` and `signature` to the verify route. Keep the `pairing` option so phone and web wallet users can sign in; draw the QR code with any QR library.

- If your page uses a bundler, the same calls work: `window.bWalletX` is set once the script tag has loaded.

- Test the server without a wallet: `const k = PrivateKey.fromRandom()`, call the challenge route with `k.toPublicKey().toString()`, sign the returned `message` with `new ProtoWallet(k).createSignature({ protocolID, keyID, counterparty: 'anyone', data: Array.from(Buffer.from(message, 'utf8')) })`, post `{ identityKey, nonce, signature }` to verify and expect success. Post the same body again and expect 401.

- Test by hand: with the bWalletX extension in Chrome, click the button and approve. Without it, scan the QR with bWalletX on a phone, check the 4-digit codes match, tap Connect, approve.

Questions: [support@bwalletx.com](mailto:support@bwalletx.com)

# Connect with bWalletX

One script gives your site a standard BRC-100 wallet. No API keys, no sign-up, and nothing passes through our servers: your page talks straight to the user's wallet.

## Get bWalletX to test with

Install the wallet you'll connect to (version 5.1.83 beta). Checksums are on each download page.

- [Chrome / Brave extension (zip)](https://bwalletx.com/download/bwalletx-extension-5.1.83.zip) · [install steps](https://bwalletx.com/extension)

- [Android APK](https://bwalletx.com/download/bwalletx-android-5.1.83.apk) · [install steps](https://bwalletx.com/android)

- [Web app](https://web.bwalletx.com) · [iPhone](https://bwalletx.com/iphone)

- [bWalletX CLI](https://bwalletx.com/cli) and [MCP server](https://bwalletx.com/mcp) for scripts and AI agents

## 1. Add the script

``<script src="https://bwalletx.com/connect.js"></script>``

## 2. Add a button

``<button id="connect">Connect with bWalletX</button>
<script>
bWalletX.button('#connect', async ({ wallet, identityKey }) => {
// wallet is a BRC-100 WalletInterface, the same API as window.CWI
console.log('Connected', identityKey);
});
</script>``

If bWalletX isn't installed, the button opens [bwalletx.com/extension](https://bwalletx.com/extension).

## 3. Use the wallet

``const { wallet } = await bWalletX.connect();

// Pay someone
await wallet.createAction({
description: 'Buy a pixel',
outputs: [{ lockingScript, satoshis: 1000, outputDescription: 'pixel' }],
});

// Sign in: prove who the user is
const { signature } = await wallet.createSignature({
data: [...new TextEncoder().encode(challenge)],
protocolID: [0, 'my site login'],
keyID: '1',
});``

## Sign users in

To let people sign in to your app with bWalletX (extension, phone or web wallet), follow the [Sign in with bWalletX guide](https://bwalletx.com/connect): one script tag (connect.js), server code, and steps for AI agents.

## Already using window.CWI?

bWalletX also sets `window.CWI`, so sites that call it directly work as they are. But if the user also has another wallet installed (such as Yours), you can't tell which one answers. `bWalletX.connect()` picks bWalletX by name (rdns `com.bwalletx.extension`) through BRC-100 wallet discovery, so it always gets the right wallet.

To list every wallet the user has and let them choose:

``const wallets = await bWalletX.discover();
// [{ info: { name, icon, rdns, kind }, wallet }, …]``

## What your site can do

bWalletX implements the BRC-100 wallet interface. Sites can request any BRC-100 action, including signatures and keys from any protocol (BRC-29 payment-key derivation included). The user approves each request; we don't keep a hidden blocklist. If we ever have to restrict something, we'll say so here and in the release notes first.

## Which address will I see?

BRC-100 wallets don't hand sites the user's main receive address. `identityKey` is the user's stable identity for your site, and payments made through `createAction` come from the user's wallet balance. So an address you derive from the identity key won't match the address shown on the wallet's Receive screen. That's expected.

## Try it

Connect with bWalletX

Questions: [support@bwalletx.com](mailto:support@bwalletx.com) · Source: [connect.js](https://bwalletx.com/connect.js)

# bWalletX MCP

Let Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor or any AI agent use your bWalletX agent accounts, within the budget and limits you set.

Claude→
ChatGPT · Cursor→
Any MCP agent

## What agents can do

### Tools (v0.2)

`accounts`, `balance`, `price`, `send` (BSV, live), `buy` (live), `strategy_show`, `strategy_load` (always on paper), `log`, `stop_all`.

### Only the accounts you give it

Agents work in agent accounts with their own keys and budget, exported from bWalletX. Your main wallet is never exposed.

### Bounded

Every spend passes the same checks as the app: the kill switch, the daily cap, at most 30 spends an hour, then the strategy's rules. An AI can only load strategies on paper; going live is a step you take yourself.

## Set up

``npm i -g bwalletx
bwalletx login --account phone # pair with your agent account in bWalletX``

Claude Code (paired: no passphrase needed, your phone signs):

``claude mcp add bwalletx -- npx -y bwalletx mcp``

Or with a key file for an unattended server:

``claude mcp add bwalletx -e BWALLETX_PASSPHRASE=your-passphrase -- npx -y bwalletx mcp``

Claude Desktop, Cursor and others (MCP config file):

``{
"mcpServers": {
"bwalletx": {
"command": "npx",
"args": ["-y", "bwalletx", "mcp"],
"env": { "BWALLETX_PASSPHRASE": "your-passphrase" }
}
}
}``

The passphrase unlocks the agent account's key file on your machine. Use a separate agent account with a small balance for AI agents. Leave the passphrase out and the server stays paper-only: it can read and practise, but never send.

# Make strategies. Sell them on the Exchange.

A strategy is a program your agent runs: when to buy, sell or send, inside limits the wallet enforces. You don’t need to code. Tell the b agent what you want and it writes the strategy, tests it against live prices, and packages it for sale. Other people buy it on Exchange › Strategies and load it into their own agent.

Tell b your idea→
b builds & tests it→
Sell it on the Exchange

## The b agent does the work

### 1 · Describe it

Say it in plain words: “slowly build up $HANDLE without chasing pumps”. b asks what it needs to know: budget, tokens, when to stop.

### 2 · b writes and tests it

b turns your answers into a strategy (goals plus exact rules) and tests it against live prices first, so you see what it would do before it trades.

### 3 · b packages it to sell

When you’re happy, publish it from the chat: b helps you fill in the listing spec, locks the program in an encrypted NFT and lists it in Exchange › Strategies at your price: one-off or limited editions. Use it yourself too.

### Or buy one

Browse Exchange › Strategies, compare specs, buy, and load it into an agent account. Resell it later like any NFT.

## Make your own, step by step

Tell the b agent what you want, for example "slowly build up $HANDLE without chasing pumps". It asks questions and turns your answers into a strategy: plain-language goals plus exact rules. Test it against live prices, then run it live in an agent account and let its results speak for it.

## Rules the wallet enforces

Every strategy has fixed limits: which tokens, how much per trade, how much per day, when to stop. The wallet checks them before anything is signed, so an agent can decide when to act but can never go past the limits.

## How selling works

### Publish & sell in one tap

When you're happy with a strategy, publish it straight from the chat and list it in Exchange › Strategies at your price, one-off or limited editions.

### Encrypted

The program is locked inside an encrypted NFT. Anyone can read the public spec; only the owner can open and run it. Resell it like any NFT.

### A spec on every listing

Sellers fill in the same spec for every strategy: what it trades, the most it spends, how often it acts, when it stops, and the seller's own risk rating. Easy to compare.

## Example strategies

Free to download. In bWalletX: Settings › Agents › your agent account › Load strategy › Choose file. Every strategy starts in test mode on live prices until you choose Run live. Change the token to one you want first.

### Slow accumulator · Medium risk

Builds a $B0ASEX position a little at a time, only while the price is low.

Buy only · $2 a trade · $10/day · $200 total · stops at 100k tokens

[Download slow-accumulator.json](https://bwalletx.com/strategies/slow-accumulator.json)

### Dip buyer · High risk

Waits for sharp dips and buys then; does nothing on quiet days.

Buy only · $5 a trade · $5/day · $50 total · stops if down 30%

[Download dip-buyer.json](https://bwalletx.com/strategies/dip-buyer.json)

### Take profit · Low risk

Sells $B0ASEX in slices once the price is above target. Never below it.

Sell / list only · at or above $0.002 · $20/day

[Download take-profit.json](https://bwalletx.com/strategies/take-profit.json)

### Allowance · Low risk

Sends a small daily BSV allowance to a fixed list of people. Edit the list first.

Send only · $1 a send · $2/day · $60 total · fixed recipients

[Download allowance.json](https://bwalletx.com/strategies/allowance.json)

Writing your own, or building tools? Read the [strategy file and listing spec](https://bwalletx.com/strategies/spec).

## Our part

Strategies are programs written and sold by users. bWalletX doesn't review, rate or recommend them. Your own b agent can suggest strategies that fit the goals you give it.

[Get bWalletX](https://bwalletx.com/get)
[All features](https://bwalletx.com/features)

# Strategy spec

The file format for bWalletX strategies, what the wallet enforces, and how strategies are sold as encrypted NFTs. Version 1.

bwalletx.strategy/1→bwalletx.strategy-nft/1

## 1. The strategy file

A strategy is a JSON file loaded into an [agent account](https://bwalletx.com/agent). One strategy per account. It has goals for the AI, rules for the wallet, a public spec, and a version.

``{
"format": "bwalletx.strategy/1",
"name": "Slow accumulator",
"version": "1.0",
"goals": "Build a position in $B0ASEX slowly. Buy small amounts a few times a day, only while the price is low. Never chase a pump: if the price runs up, wait.",
"rules": {
"tokens": [
"B0ASEX"
],
"actions": [
"buy"
],
"maxPerTradeUsd": 2,
"buyBelowUsd": 0.001,
"maxPerDayUsd": 10,
"maxTotalUsd": 200,
"stop": {
"holdTokens": 100000
}
},
"spec": {
"trades": "$B0ASEX; BSV-21 only",
"spends": "$10/day, $200 total",
"often": "A few times a day",
"stops": "Holds 100k tokens",
"needs": "Agent account with at least $20",
"risk": "Medium"
},
"changelog": [
{
"version": "1.0",
"note": "First version"
}
]
}
``

FieldRequiredMeaning

`format`yesAlways `"bwalletx.strategy/1"`.

`name`, `version`yesUp to 60 and 20 characters. Version like software: 1.0, 1.1…

`goals`yesPlain language for the AI: what to aim for and how to behave. Up to 4,000 characters.

`rules`yesExact limits the wallet enforces (section 2).

`spec`to sellThe public description buyers compare (section 4).

`changelog``[{"version","note"}]`, newest first.

Unknown fields are dropped on load, so a file can never carry instructions the wallet doesn't understand.

## 2. Rules the wallet enforces

Before any agent action is signed, the wallet checks, in order: Stop all agents and the account's own Stop, the account's daily cap, then these rules. A refused action is not signed and is written to the account's Activity log with the rule that refused it. The AI decides when and whether; it can never widen a rule.

RuleRequiredMeaning

`tokens`yesTickers or BSV-21 token ids the agent may touch. Never "any". A ticker matches the token's symbol; use the id to be exact.

`actions`yesAny of `buy`, `sell`, `send`, `list`.

`maxPerTradeUsd`yesMost one action may spend, in dollars.

`maxPerDayUsd`Most per UTC day while loaded.

`maxTotalUsd`Most in total while loaded.

`buyBelowUsd`Buy only at or below this price per token.

`sellAboveUsd`Sell or list only at or above this price per token.

`sendTo`if `send`Addresses or paymails it may send to; nobody else.

`stop.holdTokens`Finished once it holds this many of its tokens.

`stop.downPct`Finished if the account is down this % since loading.

## 3. Paper mode

Every strategy loads on paper first: live prices, a $100 simulated balance, nothing signed. Paper trades show in Activity as "Paper buy …". Run live (two taps) switches to the account's real balance. The same rules apply in both modes.

## 4. Selling: the spec

To publish, every field must be filled in. The wallet checks only that; it doesn't judge the strategy.

FieldShown asExample

`trades`What it trades$B0ASEX; BSV-21 only

`risk`Seller's risk ratingLow · Medium · High · Experimental

`spends`Most it will spend$10/day, $200 total

`often`How often it actsA few times a day

`stops`When it stopsHolds 100k tokens, or down 30%

`needs`NeedsAgent account with at least $50

## 5. Encrypted strategy NFTs

A strategy for sale is a 1Sat ordinal with content type `application/vnd.bwalletx.strategy+json`. Its content is a public envelope; the program inside is encrypted.

``{
"format": "bwalletx.strategy-nft/1",
"name": "Slow accumulator", "version": "1.0",
"description": "…",
"spec": { "trades": "…", "risk": "Medium", "spends": "…", "often": "…", "stops": "…", "needs": "…" },
"author": { "name": "…", "address": "1…" },
"sale": { "priceUsd": 5, "copies": 100, "payTo": "1…" },
"keyHash": "sha256 of the content key, hex",
"iv": "base64, 12 bytes",
"ciphertext": "base64: AES-256-GCM of the strategy file"
}``

- Publish: the author mints the first copy (the original) and gives the content key to the key service, proving they hold that copy. The key must hash to `keyHash`.

- Buy: one transaction mints the buyer's copy of the same envelope, pays `priceUsd` in BSV to `payTo`, and pays the 1% market fee.

- Unlock: the owner of a copy signs `bwalletx strategy unlock: <outpoint>: <ms timestamp>` with the key that holds it. The service checks the copy on chain (unspent, locked to that key), finds its origin, and returns the content key if the origin is the original or a paid copy within the edition size. Payment is checked against the published terms, so a re-minted envelope with a lower price is refused.

- Resell or give: send the NFT. The new owner unlocks it the same way.

Key service: `GET https://www.bwallet.space/api/strategies` lists published strategies (public envelope fields, copies sold). `?origin=<outpoint>` returns one, with the encrypted envelope. `POST` with `{"action":"publish"|"unlock", outpoint, message, pubkey_hex, signature}`.

## 6. Our part

Strategies are programs written and sold by users. bWalletX doesn't review, rate or recommend them. The wallet enforces each strategy's own rules; whether a strategy is any good is up to you.

[Strategies](https://bwalletx.com/strategies)
[CLI](https://bwalletx.com/cli)

The CLI uses the same format: `bwalletx strategy load file.json`. Source: [github.com/b0ase/bwalletx-cli](https://github.com/b0ase/bwalletx-cli). Questions: [support@bwalletx.com](mailto:support@bwalletx.com)

Source: https://bwalletx.com/blog/001-the-fork

[Development blog](https://bwalletx.com/blog) · 001 · 29–30 Sep 2026

# Forking Yours Wallet onto phones

We took the Yours Wallet browser extension and wrapped it as an iPhone and Android app with Capacitor, without rewriting its code.

## Why fork at all

Yours Wallet is an open-source BSV wallet for Chrome, released under the MIT licence by its authors. It already handled BSV, 1Sat Ordinals, BSV-21 tokens and MNEE, and it used the BRC-100 wallet standard. It had no phone app. We wanted one, and we wanted to build our own products on top of a wallet that already worked, rather than start a new one.

Our branch starts from upstream version 5.1.0 (an upstream commit dated 16 September 2026). The first commit of our own is dated 29 September 2026. Everything on this blog happened after that.

## The approach: leave upstream alone

The first commit packaged the extension as native apps with Capacitor, and it did not modify upstream's `src/` folder. Instead we added a small mobile layer:

- a stand-in for the `chrome.*` APIs that an extension expects;

- the extension's background script running in a Web Worker;

- extension pop-up windows turned into overlays inside the app;

- native storage for what the extension kept in `storage.local`.

The reason was simple: we wanted to keep taking upstream fixes. The same day we replaced some early hacks (watching the page for text, CSS overrides) with small, optional hooks, so the mobile code plugs into upstream at named points instead of fighting it. That choice paid off on 4 October, when we merged upstream's latest main, including its storage repair work, without a rewrite.

## What went in on day one

- A dApp browser inside the app, so BSV websites can talk to the wallet.

- Biometric unlock, with the password as a fallback.

- On Android: no cloud backup of app data, and screenshots blocked in release builds. On iPhone: the app-switcher snapshot is covered.

- A first TestFlight build and an Android APK, plus a small download site.

- A security review guide written for the Yours Wallet team, and the Yours-branded port shared with them. It is tagged `yours-mobile-v0.1` in our repository.

## The first real bug

On phones, the wallet could hang while starting up. The cause was duplicate rows in a sync-state table, which the extension never hit in practice. The fix shipped as iOS build 3 on the first day. It was a useful reminder that the extension's code had been tested in one environment, and a phone is a different one.

## What we owe

bWallet and bWalletX are built on Yours Wallet. We are not affiliated with its authors, and they have not endorsed our work. Their licence and credit stay in the repository. We also lean on the 1Sat tooling (`@1sat/actions`, `@1sat/templates`), the BSV wallet toolbox and Capacitor.

## What's not done

- Pinning our dependencies to upstream's lockfile works, but every upstream merge means re-pinning and re-testing.
- The mobile layer is still a shim. Anything new upstream does with `chrome.*` can break it without warning.
- Tests run on our builds. We have not had an independent security review of the mobile layer.

Related: [Features](https://bwalletx.com/features) · [Android](https://bwalletx.com/android) · [Developers](https://bwalletx.com/developers)

[Development blog](https://bwalletx.com/blog) · 002 · 30 Sep – 4 Oct 2026

# Four names in a week

Yours Wallet Mobile, bCorp Wallet, bWallet, then bWalletX. Why the name kept changing, and why there are now two apps.

## Yours Wallet Mobile

The first builds were called Yours Wallet Mobile, with an "Experimental" tag and a switch for the brand. That made sense while the port was a gift to the Yours team. It stopped making sense once we started adding our own features, because users could reasonably think the Yours authors stood behind them.

## bCorp Wallet, then bWallet

On 30 September the app ID moved to a Bitcoin Corporation one and the store build became "bCorp Wallet". The next day it became bWallet. At build time we also recoloured upstream's greens to a BSV gold, and replaced the Yours sprout with our own mark. That rename touched app IDs, the user agent string (`bWallet/1`), icons and splash screens. App IDs are hard to change once an app is in a store, so doing this early was cheap compared with doing it later.

## Two apps: bWallet and bWalletX

By 2 October it was clear that the App Store and Google Play would not accept everything we wanted to build (more on that in post 007). So we split into release channels. The store builds stay "bWallet". The private builds, with everything turned on, became bWalletX on 3 October.

The "X" itself went back and forth. First we added a small x to the b in the logo. Then the extension shipped with b+x icons. Then a flag-top b with a Space Grotesk X. On 4 October we removed the X from every logo: bWalletX is a gold b on black, and the store bWallet is a black b on yellow. The X now lives only in the name.

## Market or Exchange

The same split shows in the tab names. In bWalletX the trading tab is called Exchange. In the store app it is called Market, and it is browse-only. One setting in the code picks the label, so the two apps share the same screens.

Update, 7 Oct 2026: In the store app it is no longer called Market: the store edition, bWallet, no longer has a Market or Exchange tab at all, not even a view-only one (Apple guideline 3.1.5(iii)). Trading is only in bWalletX: see [Exchange](https://bwalletx.com/exchange).

## Was it worth it

Probably, but it cost time. Every rename meant new icons, new share images, site copy and checks that old installs still update in place. One example: the private iOS channel kept its earlier bundle ID so existing installs would update to bWalletX instead of appearing as a second app. If we did it again, we would decide the store/private split before choosing any name.

## What's not done

- Some older share images and APK file names still use earlier names.
- The store bWallet has not been approved by Apple or Google as far as our history records.

Related: [Features](https://bwalletx.com/features) · [Get bWalletX](https://bwalletx.com/get)

# Tabs, apps and a social feed

The phone layout changed many times. We added an Apps home screen with 100+ BSV apps, a Media player and a feed that reads other BSV social apps.

## The tab bar kept moving

On 1 October the tabs were Wallet, Market, Apps, Media and Settings. The same day Chat got a tab and Media moved under the wallet's NFTs. Then the tabs became Wallet, Market, Apps, Feed, Chat. On 2 October Wallet moved to the centre. On 3 October Wallet moved to the left and Apps to the centre. Each change came from using the app on a phone and finding the main action in the wrong place. We do not think the order is final.

## Apps

Apps started as two lists: our own bApps and "Other apps". It grew into a home screen with tiles, an iPhone-style arrange mode (hold, jiggle, drag) and pages for Home, bApps, Other apps and Games. Our own apps run inside the wallet in a frame and talk to it through the standard BRC-100 interface.

On 2 October we added 116 live BSV apps found through BSVRadar, and 12 from the Metanet app store. We removed one, a sat-burning stress tool, because it did not fit the rule we had set for the import. We also hid a "Buy BSV" group of on-ramp apps; it is parked until we decide how to handle it. Later, users could add their own apps, saved with their wallet so a restore brings them back.

One small correction: TokenBlaster was first listed as a bApp, then moved to Other apps on 5 October, because it is not one of ours.

## Media

The wallet sorts inscriptions by kind and plays audio and video, with a queue. It started as a tab, then became part of NFTs, then got its own button in the top bar.

## Feed

The Feed reads on-chain social posts using Bitcoin Schema (B, MAP and AIP). It also shows recent Treechat threads and Twetch posts through Twetch's public API, with a badge showing where each post came from. Posts the wallet writes itself are marked as bChat. You can lock BSV behind a post, in the style of Hodlocker, and sort by most locked. There is a leaderboard, bookmarks that sync across devices, notifications and thread views.

## What broke

- On Android, Framer Motion transforms made scrolling slow, so we turned them off app-wide.

- A spacer in the identity row squeezed the Wallet tab to zero height, which left it blank. We added error boundaries so one broken insert can't blank the whole screen.

- Bottom sheets opened behind the tab bar more than once. A test now checks every sheet.

## What's not done

- The feed polls; it does not stream new posts live.
- The app directory is curated by hand, and entries need checking again before each store submission.
- The Buy BSV group is hidden, not finished.

Related: [Features](https://bwalletx.com/features) · [Add your app](https://bwalletx.com/apps/add) · [Social](https://bwalletx.com/social)

[Development blog](https://bwalletx.com/blog) · 004 · 1–4 Oct 2026

# Names, handles and paymail

Send to $handle, name@bwalletx.com or an OpNS name. The paymail server moved domain twice, and social sign-in became a verified name.

## Sending to a name

Bitcoin addresses are hard to read aloud. On 1 October we added sending to a `$handle`, a paymail address or an OpNS name. We also added on-device OpNS mining: the phone runs the proof of work in a Web Worker and builds the mint transactions for a new name.

## Our own paymail server

We wrote a paymail server with no server keys. Names are registered with a signed request, payment destinations are derived from the wallet's public key, and incoming payments wait in an inbox until the wallet collects them.

The domain moved twice. It started on b0ase.com. The same day it moved to bwallet.space. Then we removed b0ase.com entirely, because, as the commit says, it never had DNS set up. On 4 October the address shown in the app became `name@bwalletx.com`, and bwallet.space stayed as an alias for every name.

## Choosing a handle

New wallets get a "Choose your handle" step after create or restore. Claiming a paymail name is free. The same step offers a personal `$NAME` token and room (post 005), which costs a fee and is shown before you pay.

## Continue with X or Google

On 4 October we added "Continue with X / Google" on Create Account. If you sign in, you get a verified name such as `name.x` or `name.gmail`. A plain name can be claimed by anyone; a verified name shows that the person behind it controls that X or Google account.

The design changed during the day. First the chat server (bit-sign) handled the sign-in. Then we moved it to bWalletX's own server, and bit-sign keeps nothing: it only confirms the sign-in ticket. Then we decided one wallet has one identity, and a verified social name always wins over a plain one.

Social sign-in is off in the store build, pending Apple's guideline 4.8 on sign-in options.

## A detail that took longer than expected

Placeholder names such as "Anonymous" or "Account 1" kept showing up in places where a real name should be. We now never show them; the paymail name is used instead.

## What's not done

- Handles are not tradeable yet. The numbered accounts and tradeable handles spec is design only.
- Name resolution depends on our paymail server being up.
- Social sign-in is not in the store build.

Related: [Social](https://bwalletx.com/social) · [Features](https://bwalletx.com/features)

[Development blog](https://bwalletx.com/blog) · 005 · 1–5 Oct 2026

# Personal tokens and token rooms

Hold a token to enter its chat room. Your $NAME is a token with its own room. How rooms, tickets and issuers came together, and what we reversed.

## The idea

Every token can have a chat room, and holding the token gets you in. To invite someone, you send them the token. Your own `$NAME` is a token too, so you have a room that people enter by holding some of your token. The room's owner sets the rules: how many tokens to enter, and whether you just hold them or spend them per message, per minute or per day, burned or sent back to the issuer.

## A reversal on DMs

On 1 October we went all in: Chat became token rooms only, and we removed direct messages and new-chat-by-handle from the interface. On 2 October we added DMs back, with a merged contact list. People need to message one person without first buying a token. Open rooms came the same day (post 007).

## Minting, and another reversal

The Mint sheet briefly had "Mint a chatroom" as the first option. We then removed "Mint a token", on the grounds that a token is a room. The same day we put it back. People do want to mint a token without thinking about chat.

## Tickets

We wrote a spec for tickets: tokens that are burned to enter a room, checked at zero confirmations so entry takes seconds, not blocks. The server can verify a ticket burn from the transaction itself before it is mined. For a while the wallet had a Tickets tab. On 3 October we dropped it: tickets are just tokens that get burned on entry, so they appear under Tokens.

## Who issued this token?

Anyone can deploy a token with any ticker, so a ticker proves nothing. Since 2 October every mint from the wallet carries a signed issuer statement in the same transaction, in a separate output so 1Sat indexing is not affected. The wallet checks the signature and shows "Issued by $handle". When several tokens share a ticker, it says so.

## Only the issuer sets the rules

At first, whoever created a room could edit it. On 5 October we changed this: room settings can be changed only by the token's issuer, proved by signing with the key behind the issuer address. A wallet that holds that key can "Claim admin". Everyone else sees the room rules read-only.

## Bounties

Token rooms got a Bounties sheet: work posted in a room, paid in the room's token when it is merged. This is early and lightly used.

## What's not done

- Token rooms are hidden in the store build.
- Chat polls the server every few seconds; it is not live yet (see the bChat plan in post 007).
- Numbered accounts and tradeable handles are specified but not built.

Related: [Social](https://bwalletx.com/social) · [Exchange](https://bwalletx.com/exchange)

[← 004 Names, handles and paymail](https://bwalletx.com/blog/004-names-and-paymail)[006 Who pays for indexing →](https://bwalletx.com/blog/006-paying-for-indexing)

Source: https://bwalletx.com/blog/006-paying-for-indexing

[Development blog](https://bwalletx.com/blog) · 006 · 1–4 Oct 2026

# Who pays for indexing

A BSV-21 token only shows up in wallets once an indexer lists it. Working out who pays for that, and how much, took four attempts.

## The problem

BSV-21 tokens rely on an overlay indexer to track balances. The 1Sat overlay wants a token's funding address topped up before it indexes it. If nobody pays, the token exists on chain but wallets don't show it.

## Attempt one: a small pre-fund

At first the wallet sent a few thousand sats to the indexer when you minted. On 1 October we added reminders and a "Finish setting up" card for unpaid tokens, with one-tap pay under $0.10.

## Attempt two: the real minimum

On 3 October we found that since 2 October the indexer lists a token only once its balance reaches a minimum of 10,000,000 sats (0.1 BSV). Our 3,000-sat pre-fund had listed nothing. So we changed minting to pay the full minimum, and showed the real figure in every quote.

## Attempt three: make it optional

0.1 BSV is a lot to ask from someone minting a personal token on day one. The same day, minting stopped paying for indexing. Instead the wallet remembers your token and offers "Set up $X's room": the indexer minimum plus a bCorp fee in one transaction, with a "Not now" option.

Update, 7 Oct 2026: The bCorp fee now applies only to the token's issuer. Someone who holds a token they didn't create pays only the indexing cost (post [015](https://bwalletx.com/blog/015-launchpad)).

## Attempt four: say what it is

On 4 October we changed the wording: the room's indexer minimum is a prepaid deposit that the indexer draws on, not a fee that disappears. That is closer to how it works.

## Empty wallets

New users have no BSV, so they could not even pay the network fee to mint their personal token. bCorp now sponsors that: if minting fails only for lack of a fee, the app asks our server for a small gift to the wallet's own address, then tries again. The user's wallet still signs its own mint. The server has a daily cap.

## Credits, shelved

We also built Credits ($BCREDIT), an in-app balance for paying bCorp services. On 2 October we shelved it in every build. The code is still there, but nothing opens it. Paying directly in BSV was simpler to explain, and simpler for the stores.

## Prices in dollars

One rule came out of this: prices are set and shown in US dollars, and users pay in sats at the live rate. Sats appear at payment time or as small secondary text.

## What's not done

- Indexing costs are set by a third party and can change without notice, as they did on 2 October.
- A token whose room is never set up stays invisible to most wallets.
- The sponsor has a daily cap; when it runs out, new users have to fund their own fee.

Related: [Social](https://bwalletx.com/social) · [Exchange](https://bwalletx.com/exchange)

[Development blog](https://bwalletx.com/blog) · 007 · 2–5 Oct 2026

# Store rules, open rooms and moderation

We audited the app against App Store and Play rules, split it into four release channels and built the safety features the stores require.

## The audit

On 2 October we wrote a store audit that checks the wallet against Apple's App Review Guidelines and Google Play's policies. It flagged trading, paying the developer from inside the app, user-generated content without moderation, AI features without consent, and missing account deletion.

## One code base, four channels

A build switch turns the store rules on. Then we split into four channels with separate app IDs: iOS store, Android Play, iOS private and Android direct. The store channels keep the store rules. The private channels have everything on and are now bWalletX. A private build installs beside a store build on the same phone.

## Going back and forth on the Market

The store build first had a view-only Market. Later on 2 October we let it keep the token wallet: minting, peer-to-peer trading and indexing, with no bCorp fees. On 3 October we made the store Market view-only again, citing Apple guideline 3.1.5(iii) on cryptocurrency exchanges. The store build also dropped the investor share offers we had prototyped; that panel was removed from every build.

Update, 7 Oct 2026: Since then the store edition, bWallet, no longer has a Market or Exchange tab at all, not even a view-only one (Apple guideline 3.1.5(iii)). Trading is only in bWalletX: see [Exchange](https://bwalletx.com/exchange).

## What the stores require, and we built

- Account deletion. Settings explains what is deleted and what can't be (anything on chain), then removes the paymail name, the chat account and local data.

- User content. Terms you agree to before Feed, Chat and Calls. Report and Block on messages, profiles and rooms.

- AI consent. A consent sheet before the first b agent message, saying what is sent and to whom.

## Open rooms

Token rooms are hidden in the store build, so the store app needed rooms that anyone can join. Open rooms shipped on 2 October in every build: public or invite-only, with owners and moderators who can remove members, delete messages and close a room. Reports go to one shared report system on the server.

## Chat speed, honestly

Our 5 October bChat plan says it plainly: chat feels slow because it asks the server for new messages every 4 seconds inside a room and every 30 seconds on the list, and nothing is stored on the phone. The plan is local message storage, a live connection, instant display of your own messages and push notifications, and moving the chat server into its own open-source repository.

## What's not done

- Neither store build has been approved, as far as our history records.
- Someone has to review reports every day. That is a process, not code, and it needs an owner.
- Chat is still polling. The bChat plan is a plan.

Related: [Features](https://bwalletx.com/features) · [Privacy](https://bwalletx.com/privacy) · [Social](https://bwalletx.com/social)

Source: https://bwalletx.com/blog/008-the-exchange

[Development blog](https://bwalletx.com/blog) · 008 · 1–5 Oct 2026

# Building the Exchange, and why buys broke

Listing and buying 1Sat tokens from the wallet. Most of the work was not the screens but storage limits, double-encrypted records and slow APIs.

## The first Market

On 1 October the Market showed trending 1Sat tokens and collections with an in-app buy, and NFT categories for music, video and images. Adult content is blurred or hidden by a filter that is always on. Selling was hidden at first, because upstream had turned off creating OrdLock listings.

## Buys that didn't work

On 3 October we fixed buying. Three things were wrong: the format of the listing reference, a step in the wallet's permission module that never finished, and the size of the unlocking script. Then bought tokens did not show on the Wallet tab, because they never reached the indexer.

Then a deeper problem. Quick, unconfirmed spends one after another hit "Maximum BEEF depth exceeded. Limit is 12". We raised the limit to 64. The first fix did not reach the copy of the toolbox that threw the error, so we patched every bundled copy at build time. The real fix was storage: wallets that kept their active storage on 1Sat's remote service now switch to the device, with 1Sat as a backup.

## Storage, and a restore bug we caused

Moving to device storage exposed more. Backups over 1 MB were rejected by the remote service, so big wallets had never backed up. We now sync in chunks of about 400 KB. Then we found new and restored wallets starting on device storage could not find their history. They now start on 1Sat storage, then switch to the device once.

## Tokens that were bought but missing

Some bought tokens never showed in balances. Their records had been encrypted twice, and the toolbox removed only one layer, so it found no amount and skipped them. We fixed the decryption and added "Find missing tokens", which re-derives the keys used for market buys and picks up anything the wallet owns.

## Selling, and speed

On 4 October Sell came back, listing tokens as OrdLock v2, since v1 creation is off upstream. The wallet can still read and cancel v1 listings. Token listings now come from GorillaPool's market API, which answered in about 0.9 s against 7 to 15 s for the search we used before. On 5 October we added retries and a fallback when api.1sat.app has problems, instead of showing an empty list.

## Exchange today

In bWalletX the tab is called Exchange. It has category filters, search by ticker or token id, price charts from recent sales, and sections for Strategies (post 010) and Contracts and Bonds (post 011). Token rows have Buy, Sell, Send and Chat. In the store app it is Market and view-only.

Update, 7 Oct 2026: The store app no longer has a view-only Market: the store edition, bWallet, no longer has a Market or Exchange tab at all, not even a view-only one (Apple guideline 3.1.5(iii)). Trading is only in bWalletX: see [Exchange](https://bwalletx.com/exchange).

## What's not done

- Trading depends on third-party indexers and APIs (1Sat, GorillaPool). When they are slow or wrong, so is the Exchange.
- The chart is built from recent sales only; thin markets give misleading charts.
- We have not had the trading code reviewed independently.

Related: [Exchange](https://bwalletx.com/exchange) · [Strategies](https://bwalletx.com/exchange/strategies)

[← 007 Store rules, open rooms and moderation](https://bwalletx.com/blog/007-store-and-private)[009 The b agent: paid, or your own key →](https://bwalletx.com/blog/009-the-b-agent)

---

Source: https://bwalletx.com/blog/009-the-b-agent

[Development blog](https://bwalletx.com/blog) · 009 · 1–5 Oct 2026

# The b agent: paid, or your own key

An assistant inside the wallet. It started free, became paid-only within a day, and now asks for consent before it sends anything.

## The first version

On 1 October the b in the centre of the top bar opened the b agent: a chat page built on the chat server's compose feature. It was free to use. Free AI costs us money with no limit, so it did not last.

## Paid only

On 2 October we removed the free path. There are now two ways to use the agent:

- Your own key. You add an API key for Anthropic, OpenAI or OpenRouter. It stays in secure storage on your device, and requests go straight from your phone to that provider. We don't see them.

- Pay per message in BSV. The wallet asks for a quote, pays and gets the answer, with a daily limit. The price is set in US dollars and converted to sats at quote time. These messages go through our server to Anthropic.

We also cut the history sent with each message from 20 turns to 8. That lowers cost and sends less of your conversation.

## Consent

For the stores, and because it is right, the agent now shows a consent sheet before the first message to each provider. It says what is sent (your message and the last 8 turns) and what isn't. You can revoke consent in Settings. The agent also refuses input that looks like a recovery phrase or a private key.

On 5 October we added a banner on the agent page to add your own key, since that is the more private option.

## What it can do

The agent has a usage guide for the wallet as its system prompt, so it can explain features. In agent accounts it can act, buying and sending, but only through the strategy rules the wallet enforces (post 010). Quick-start buttons cover the common cases: create a strategy, trade with a strategy, buy or sell one.

## What's not done

- The store build allows only your own key; pay-per-message is a private-build feature.
- The agent can be wrong. Any action it takes in an agent account is limited by the strategy gate, not by its judgement.
- There is no long-term memory, by design, and no way yet to export a conversation.

Related: [Agents](https://bwalletx.com/agent) · [Strategies](https://bwalletx.com/strategies)

[← 008 Building the Exchange, and why buys broke](https://bwalletx.com/blog/008-the-exchange)[010 Agent accounts, strategies, CLI and MCP →](https://bwalletx.com/blog/010-agents-strategies-cli)

---

Source: https://bwalletx.com/blog/010-agents-strategies-cli

[Development blog](https://bwalletx.com/blog) · 010 · 4–5 Oct 2026

# Agent accounts, strategies, CLI and MCP

Separate wallet accounts for agents, spending rules the wallet enforces, a market for strategies, and a command-line tool that keeps keys on the phone.

## Agent accounts

On 4 October we added a switch when you add an account: Agent account. An agent account is a separate wallet that you fund from your main one. Settings has Stop all, a stop per account, a daily cap, Sweep back for tokens, NFTs and BSV, and an activity log. The idea is that an agent can never spend more than you put in its account.

## Strategies

A strategy is a file that says what an agent may do: which tokens, how much, how often, within what limits. The wallet enforces the limits, not the agent. You load a strategy into an agent account, and the b agent can then buy and send there, through that gate.

We first called the dry-run mode "paper mode", with paper fills. On 5 October the site wording changed to "test on live prices", because "paper" and "pretend money" undersold what it does: it uses real market prices without spending.

## Selling strategies

Strategies can be sold on Exchange › Strategies as encrypted NFTs. A buyer pays the author plus a 1% fee, gets their own copy minted, unlocks it through our key service and loads it. Since the key service releases the content, buyers depend on it staying up.

## Running agents on a computer

There are two ways to run an agent account from a laptop or server with the `bwalletx` CLI, which is published on npm, along with an MCP server for AI tools:

- Pairing. Scan a QR code with the phone. The pairing is bound to one agent account, with scopes and an expiry of at most 30 days. Requests run on the phone through the agent gate, so keys never leave it.

- Key export. For a server with no phone, export a passphrase-encrypted key file. This works only for agent accounts, never for your main wallet.

The CLI pages describe v0.1 and then v0.2, which added pairing and live buys.

## What's not done

- Strategies are new. We have no track record of how they behave over weeks.
- The strategy key service is ours and centralised; if it is down, bought strategies can't be unlocked.
- Spec items such as per-agent rate limits and scoped agent tokens are partly built; check the spec page for what is live.
- Nothing here is financial advice, and agents can lose money within their limits.

Related: [Agents](https://bwalletx.com/agent) · [Strategies](https://bwalletx.com/strategies) · [Strategy spec](https://bwalletx.com/strategies/spec) · [CLI](https://bwalletx.com/cli) · [MCP](https://bwalletx.com/mcp) · [Exchange › Strategies](https://bwalletx.com/exchange/strategies)

Source: https://bwalletx.com/blog/011-pnees-pilot

[Development blog](https://bwalletx.com/blog) · 011 · 4–5 Oct 2026

# From a dollar bond to PNEEs on mainnet

A BSV-backed dollar token went from a design note to a small, capped mainnet pilot in two days. This is what is enforced, what is not, and what went wrong.

## Contracts and bonds

On 4 October we wrote a design for a "$1 bond": lock BSV in a vault and mint dollar tokens against it. On 5 October the wallet got Exchange › Contracts and Bonds, where contract descriptions are published as public NFTs.

## The prototype

The vault and token contracts are written in sCrypt in a separate repository. A vault holds BSV, mints against it up to a set ratio, lets the owner close it by handing the tokens back, and lets anyone liquidate it below 150% using a price signed by 3 of 5 signers (the median of the 3). There are 22 local tests, run through the Bitcoin Script interpreter.

We could not run it on testnet. On 5 October no faucet we tried could give us test coins: one returned an error, and the others were unreachable or needed a captcha.

## Bonds became Penny Notes, then PNEEs

The same day we changed the design. These are not bonds; they are cash. One unit is one cent. Vaults start at 10x collateral, so $1 of BSV mints 10 cents, and a vault survives an 85% fall in BSV. The notes became an ordinary BSV-21 token, $PNEE, with 2 decimals, so any 1Sat-compatible wallet can hold them. The name settled as PNEEs (Penny Stablecoins).

## The mainnet pilot

Mainnet runs only in a pilot mode with hard caps in code: about $5 of collateral per vault, $10 across all vaults, $2 of notes per vault, and a fee cap per transaction. Every broadcast prints a summary and needs "broadcast" typed to confirm. Plain mainnet mode is refused. The first vault locked 12,500,000 sats; the first mint was 25 PNEEs against a 3-of-5 price of $20.32. The transaction IDs are on the [PNEEs page](https://bwalletx.com/pnees).

## What went wrong

- Reused coins. We were picking coins from WhatsOnChain's unspent list, which can lag behind. That let the tool try to spend a coin that had already been spent, and WhatsOnChain's broadcast did not report the double spend clearly. We now broadcast through ARC first, which reports double spends as errors, and keep a local list of spent coins.

- Missing notes. WhatsOnChain's address index skips inscription outputs, so notes didn't show up. We added a local ledger of notes.

- Indexing. The 1Sat overlay did not index PNEEs straight away, even after we paid its funding template. The wallet now shows PNEEs from GorillaPool, labelled "Indexing", until the overlay catches up.

## The trust gaps

The vault script can't check other inputs, so it can't prove that real notes were burned when a vault closes. For now bCorp, as issuer, co-signs releases and burns, in public on chain. That means the issuer could refuse to co-sign a liquidation. All five price signers are run by us during the pilot, so they are not independent. A liquidator can also choose an old transaction lock time, which weakens the price freshness check. The prototype's README lists these in full.

Note transfers themselves need no co-signer. Releases and burns do.

## What's not done

- Independent price signers.
- An on-chain check that burned notes are real, replacing the issuer co-signer. Shieldpool is one route we are watching; it is testnet only.
- The stability pool (backers earn from liquidations) is design only.
- A testnet run, and a review of the scripts, before any meaningful amount.
- Wallet screens for opening and closing vaults. The PNEEs card is there; vault management is not.
- Legal review before the stability pool opens to the public. Store editions stay browse-only.

Related: [PNEEs](https://bwalletx.com/pnees) · [Exchange](https://bwalletx.com/exchange)

# The extension, the web app and pairing

bWalletX also runs as a Chrome and Brave extension and as a web app. On iPhone the web app is the only way to get the full wallet, so we made backup mandatory there.

## Back to an extension

Since the code started as an extension, building one again was cheap. On 1 October we branded it; on 3 October it shipped as bWalletX, with the full mobile interface in Chrome's side panel and a gold strip to open it full screen. We serve it from this site, not the Chrome Web Store, so you install it in developer mode. Brave works too.

Two fixes mattered. Each version used to install with a new extension ID, which meant a new, empty wallet. Since 5.1.9 a fixed key in the manifest keeps the same ID across versions. And on the question of who answers websites: on 3 October the extension set `window.CWI` only if no other wallet had. The next day we reversed that: bWalletX takes it by default, even over Yours, and a setting hands it back.

## Letting websites find the wallet

Websites can discover bWalletX through BRC-100 wallet announcements, in the style of EIP-6963. A small `connect.js` on the [Developers page](https://bwalletx.com/developers) shows how. For desktop sites and a phone wallet, there is phone pairing: scan a code, check the same 4-digit code on both screens, and requests travel through an encrypted relay that stores nothing. Each request still needs approval on the phone.

## The web app, and iPhone

The web wallet runs at web.bwalletx.com. On iPhone, Apple only allows App Store apps, and the store edition can't trade. So bWalletX on iPhone is the web app, added to the Home Screen from Safari.

The iPhone page says it plainly: the keys are on your phone, not our servers, but browser storage is fragile. Safari can clear it. On 5 October we asked the browser for persistent storage, and added a mandatory backup step. After you create or restore a wallet, you save an encrypted backup or write down your recovery phrase and pass a three-word quiz. Receive waits until you have backed up. The only way to skip is "remind me later" at zero balance. In the native apps and the extension the step can be skipped.

## What's not done

- The extension is not in the Chrome Web Store.
- Persistent storage is a request; Safari may still clear site data. A backup is the only protection.
- Pairing depends on our relay being up.

Related: [Extension](https://bwalletx.com/extension) · [iPhone](https://bwalletx.com/iphone) · [Developers](https://bwalletx.com/developers) · [Android](https://bwalletx.com/android)

# Two sites from one

A download page became bwallet.space, then bwalletx.com became the main site, with the store site generated from it. And this blog.

## From a download page to two sites

The first site, on 29 September, was a download page for the Yours-branded port, with an Android APK and a TestFlight link. On 1 October it became the bWallet site at bwallet.space, with section videos, a beta APK and a waitlist.

On 3 October we forked it to make bwalletx.com. Over the next two days bwalletx.com became the main site, with pages for features, Exchange, Social, Agents, Strategies, CLI, MCP, Android, iPhone, Extension, Developers and PNEEs, each with its own share image.

## Keeping the store site clean

bwallet.space is the site for the store app, and it must not advertise features the store app doesn't have. Since 4 October a script copies the shared assets from bwalletx.com and generates the bwallet.space home page from ours, with trading, token rooms and social sign-in taken out and clear links to bwalletx.com. Pages that exist only on bWalletX redirect there. The script never copies HTML pages, so this blog is not copied to the store site.

## Navigation

The navbar was rewritten by hand on every page until 5 October, when one script, `nav.js`, started rendering it from a single config for both sites. Each section can have its own sub-menu. That is where this blog lives: under Developers.

## Small things that went wrong

- The waitlist form 404'd on bwalletx.com until we proxied it to bwallet.space.

- X kept old share images, so several images have version numbers in their file names to break the cache.

- The big b logo was hidden under the fixed header on sub-pages until we added spacing.

- We dropped a Brave Shields tip from the extension page because we hadn't verified it.

## About this blog

These posts were written from the git history of the wallet, this site, the chat server and the PNEEs prototype. They are as accurate as the commits allow. If something here is wrong, the code is the record, and we will correct the post.

## What's not done

- The two sites still share one API host; bwalletx.com proxies some requests to bwallet.space.
- The APK download folder keeps every version; there is no cleanup yet.

[Development blog](https://bwalletx.com/blog) · 014 · 6 Oct 2026

# One feed for BSV

Every BSV social app keeps its own feed. bChat shows all of them, credits them, and pays the people who wrote the posts.

## The odd thing about BSV social apps

Everything you post on Twetch, Treechat, Peck or Fwetch goes on-chain. It's public. Anyone can read it.

And yet each app only shows its own posts. You need a separate app, account and wallet for each one, and a writer on one app never reaches the readers on another.

That's a Web2 habit. On Twitter or Reddit the company owns the posts, so walling them in makes sense for the company. On BSV nobody owns the posts except the people who wrote them. The walls are only around the indexers.

## What bChat does

[bitcoinchat.online/feed](https://www.bitcoinchat.online/feed) shows posts from Twetch, Treechat, Peck, Fwetch and bChat in one timeline.

- Every post has a badge saying where it came from, and a link back to the original.

- You can like, reply and tip from bChat. Your reply is a bChat post that points at the original; we never post as another app.

- Tips go straight to the author's own address. bChat takes nothing.

Update, 7 Oct 2026: Where each source is read from now: bChat posts from bWalletX’s own indexer (push.bwalletx.com/feed), merged with bmap; Twetch from Twetch’s own public read API, since bmap stopped indexing Twetch; Treechat from the overlay at overlay.peck.to, since bmap stopped indexing it; Peck from the same overlay; and Fwetch (fwetch.lol) from its public API, since its posts aren’t Bitcoin Schema and no general indexer reads them.

## Authors first

The rule we've written down is simple: a post belongs to the person who wrote it, not to the app they wrote it in.

- Any app can show any author's post, with credit and a link home.

- Authors get paid wherever their post is read.

- If an author hides their own post (a signed "hide" from the same key), every app that follows the spec hides it.

- An app can't stop another app showing public posts. If it wants something kept private, it can keep it off-chain.

## Apps get paid too

When a bChat user tips a post that came from another app, bChat adds 5% on top for that app, in the same transaction. The author still gets the full tip.

So a $0.05 tip on a Treechat post pays the author $0.05 and Treechat $0.0025. Treechat earns from its posts being read in bChat without doing anything.

That's the bit I think the other apps haven't seen yet. Syndication isn't someone taking your content. It's your content earning in more places.

## What we need from the other apps

Two small things:

- A payment address for each author on each post. Some apps post everything from one shared address, so a tip can't reach the right person. That's why tips on Treechat posts are switched off in bChat for now.

- A payment address for the app itself, for the 5% share.

And if they want to show bChat posts back, with a bChat badge, it's one line of code.

## Join

The format is an open spec: [bitcoinchat.online/docs/feed-protocol](https://www.bitcoinchat.online/docs/feed-protocol)

There's a free public indexer and a drop-in embed:

``<script src="https://www.bitcoinchat.online/embed/feed.js" data-source="all"></script>``

If you build a BSV app with a feed, come and talk to us in the [bWallet Lounge on bChat](https://www.bitcoinchat.online/room/LOUNGE), or email [support@bwalletx.com](mailto:support@bwalletx.com).

— Richard

Related: [Social](https://bwalletx.com/social) · [Developers](https://bwalletx.com/developers) · [003 Tabs, apps and a social feed](https://bwalletx.com/blog/003-tabs-apps-feed)
